newsitem.title: USA: MCI loss warning seen as political salvo.
newsitem.headline: MCI loss warning seen as political salvo.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp.'s call for speedy regulatory action to open local phone markets -- backed by a profit warning to prove its point -- escalates a long-running war of words between long-distance carriers and local service providers.
Analysts said MCI's comments were mostly a political move designed to pressure regulators to take action to speed the entry of new competitors into the local phone business.

The company said late Thursday that heavy spending to enter local phone markets would hurt earnings for the rest of 1997 and 1998. The news sent the stocks of MCI and merger partner British Telecommunications Plc tumbling Friday.
MCI fell $7.125 to $35.25 in heavy trading on Nasdaq. BT's American shares fell $5.25 to $76.31 in New York.

"This is such a dramatic announcement," SBC Warburg analyst Barry Sine said. "It got Wall Street's attention and it certainly has to be heard by (Federal Communications Commission) Chairman Reed Hundt."
Sine said MCI's warning may even be a prelude to an antitrust case against the regional Bell companies that continue to dominate U.S. local phone markets.
The tactic could lead to a replay of the court action MCI brought against AT&T Corp. in the 1970s that led to the breakup of the Bell system in 1984, he said.

But other analysts said the heavy investments MCI is making to enter the local phone business, with its resulting tug on profits, are nothing new and that the announcement was merely the latest political volley aimed at regulators.

"MCI is looking for federal regulators to rescue it from the predicaments of the 1996 Telecom Act, but there's only so much the FCC can do," said Scott Cleland, regulatory analyst at broker Legg Mason's Precursor Group, referring to the law that opened up competition in local markets to long-distance companies and allowed local phone companies to offer long-distance service.
MCI said its investments in local service could mean losses of more than $800 million, or double previous estimates -- and 1998 losses could be even greater.

In its request for regulatory action, MCI blamed what it called the "anti-competitve" practices of the Baby Bells that dominate local phone markets, including foot-dragging on talks to open up local phone networks and computer systems.

The company asked the Federal Communications Commission to take action to end the logjam. Eighteen months after the telecommunications reform law was passed, the vast majority of Americans still have no choice when it comes to picking a local phone company, consultants Yankee Group said recently.

"What they may be trying is to stiffen the back of the FCC on Bell entry into long-distance requests," Cleland said of pressures from Baby Bells on allowing them into the long-distance business. "The big thing the FCC can do is to keep the Bells out of long distance until the Baby Bells do more to open their local phone markets," he said.

"The RBOCs have to be careful here," Sine agreed, referring to the regional Bell, or Baby Bell, local operating companies. "They need MCI to be successful here if they are ever are going to get into the long-distance business."

Sine said MCI may try to use the threat of an antitrust lawsuit as a sledgehammer to increase its bargaining power with Baby Bells in negotiations aimed at allowing MCI to interconnect with existing local networks.
"There would be no shortage of co-plaintiffs if MCI filed an antitrust suit against the Baby Bells," Sine said.
MCI's woes echo those of long-time adversary AT&T Corp., which said in March that heavy investments required to enter local service and other new markets would hurt earnings.
The burden of financing MCI's entry into local phone markets also figured heavily in arguments MCI has used to win approval for its pending merger with British Telecom.

But BellSouth Corp., a regional Bell company that faces competition from MCI and other new entrants in its nine-state local service market, said MCI is figuring out that it is expensive to operate a local phone network.
"Any start-up business tends to lose money at the beginning," BellSouth Chief Financial Officer Ron Dykes said.

"The remarkable part of this saga is MCI's brazen attempt to turn this fact of business life into something more than it is in order to gain political advantage. Regulators shouldn't be fooled by this ploy," he said.
